title: Noah's Secret Science Code
markdown:
Dawn broke like a popped cork and spilled gold across Noah’s room. Birdsong started the day whether he was ready or not. The Junior Science Fair hummed in his head. His project — states of matter — was almost ready. Ice cube, puddle, steam: the three familiar pictures were already pinned. Better: Auntie Jo, scientist and maker of whimsical post, had sent a secret note.

He bounced. Maple the hare was already at the window, whiskers going, ears up. “What’s the buzz?”

“Auntie Jo.” He unfolded the crinkled envelope. Letters, but jumbled. “X L F N G K R G.” It sounded like a sneeze.

Maple hopped closer. “A new crunchy carrot? Flying giggling pickles?”

Noah’s brow furrowed. Auntie Jo always sent hints for the fair. Last year it had been a riddle about magnets that he had solved too late, standing in the hall with a paperclip still in his pocket. “A message. I can’t read it.” Shoulders drooped. The mystery sat there, unsolved, while the project board waited half-drawn.

He paced. Feet tapped. Gaze hit the forgotten notebook under the desk — dewdrop sparkle, cloud types, neat columns. Near the back, a small box: ABC becoming DEF. The Caesar cipher. She had shown him on a rainy Thursday, using the kitchen table as a chalkboard. Each letter three places forward. To hide, shift ahead. To read, shift back.

The spark arrived. Heart thumped. “If she moved them forward three, we move them back three.”

Maple leaned in, ears flattening to concentrate. Noah counted on his fingers so he would not skip.

X: W, V, U. U.
L: K, J, I. I.
F: C.
N: K.
G: D.
K: H.
R: O.
Last G: F, E, D. D.

He wrote it once, slowly: U I C K D H O D.

“Quick D Hod?” Maple tilted. “A super-fast hop? A fluffy cloud?”

Noah shook his head. The letters sat like a word that had not decided where to break. He looked at the board: ice, water, steam — and the extra card he had not used yet, the one about a solid that skipped the puddle. Auntie Jo loved a rhyme that was also a fact. He grouped the letters again, not by guessing a new shift, just by listening to them.

“QUICK. DRY. ICE.”

He leapt. “Solid carbon dioxide straight to gas. Sublimation. That’s the missing piece of the project.”

Maple bounced. “A secret that is also science.”

He grabbed the materials: gloves, a warning card in large letters, a space on the board for fog instead of another melting cube. The fair would get a show that was not only pictures of ice cubes becoming puddles. He did not announce that the adventure was beginning. He put the decoded scrap in the notebook next to ABC/DEF, so the next hint, if it came, would have a place to land. Maple twitched toward the door. The birds, unimpressed by ciphers, kept singing.
